statements.quote: it's entirely within the role of possible that the Streisand Effect ... gets renamed the Lamar effect before this is all done
statements.context: Opening of a post about UnitedHealth Group (UHG) hiring defamation firm Clare Locke to send a threatening letter to plastic surgeon Elisabeth Potter over her Instagram/TikTok claims about a mid-surgery prior-authorization call. The author expects the legal threat to backfire and spread the story further (Streisand effect), jokingly renamed the Lamar effect after the Drake/Kendrick Lamar dispute.
statements.confidence_phrase: entirely within the role of possible
statements.note: Hyperbole: the literal renaming is a joke; the sincere expectation is that UHG's legal threat backfires and amplifies Potter's claims. Footnote marker skipped with ' ... '.

statements.quote: why I think this United case against a physician is a loser, from a legal standpoint
statements.context: Thesis of the post. UHG, through Clare Locke, sent a defamation threat letter to Dr. Elisabeth Potter. The author judges that any defamation case UHG brings against her would lose in court.
statements.note: Restated as 'why this is such a loser of a case for UHG'. Legal-outcome call conditional on a suit being filed.

statements.quote: Thus, the defense of this particular physician would cost her zero dollars, unless maybe, if she lost, she would have to pay up. But more likely, the defense would be covered by a third-party like Chubb.
statements.context: The author asserts that defamation defenses are almost always covered by the defendant's homeowners insurance, so Dr. Potter's defense against a UHG suit would cost her nothing and would most likely be paid by an insurer such as Chubb.
statements.note: Conditional on UHG filing suit.

statements.quote: This is a horrible state of affairs, because it makes it endlessly more likely that there will be more political violence against healthcare executives
statements.context: Aside about the celebrity treatment Luigi Mangione (accused of killing the UnitedHealthcare CEO) receives in prison. The author predicts this makes further political violence against healthcare executives more likely.
statements.note: Compound sentence; continues into the hunker-down prediction logged separately.

statements.quote: it's only going get them to hunker down, ensuring that only the most profit driven and antisocial individuals choose to take the next open job at the healthcare behemoth
statements.context: Same aside on violence against executives. The author restates his earlier argument that the threat of violence will make insurers hunker down, so only the most profit-driven and antisocial people will take the next open executive job at UHG.
statements.note: Restatement of an earlier call ('as I've argued before').

statements.quote: If this case were to go to court, it would be determined by a jury, and if you can find a jury of 12 Americans who are willing to let united off the hook and penalize a doctor, for saying something, anything about United? Good luck.
statements.context: Conditional call: if UHG's defamation case against Dr. Potter went to a jury trial, the author expects no jury of 12 Americans would side with UHG against a doctor.
statements.note: Rhetorical 'Good luck' carries the confidence; reads as near-certain that UHG would lose before a jury.

statements.quote: Were they to file this as a lawsuit, the doctor would immediately move to file an anti-SLAPP motion (if she lives in a state, like NYS, with this kind of law).
statements.context: Conditional prediction of Dr. Potter's legal response if UHG files a defamation suit: an immediate anti-SLAPP (strategic lawsuit against public participation) motion. The author later repeats that this is 'the obvious first step for the doctor in question should a lawsuit be filed'.
statements.note: Conditional on filing and on the doctor's state having an anti-SLAPP law.

statements.quote: They're actually establishing, in their threatening letter, the grounds for dismissing their subsequent case, because it is very clearly aimed at limiting the public participation of the physician to speak out against the practices of United.
statements.context: The author argues the Clare Locke letter itself supplies the grounds to dismiss any later UHG suit as a SLAPP. He adds that it would be impossible to argue the matter is not one of public concern.
statements.note: Predicts dismissal grounds for a not-yet-filed case.

statements.quote: Essentially, by saying “it was your error” united is establishing the non-maliciousness of the statement on the part of the doctor, which would make their subsequent case, which should be clear they haven't filed yet, impossible to win.
statements.context: The author reasons that UHG's letter, by blaming the dispute on the doctor's ordering mistake, undercuts any showing of actual malice, so a future defamation case by UHG against Dr. Potter would be impossible to win.
statements.note: Conditional on a suit being filed.

statements.quote: It is impossible to believe this case, if it were ever filed, would not be dismissed as a blatant strategic lawsuit against public participation, but most importantly, beyond that, if it ever went to trial, the whole matter would be subject to relentless discovery.
statements.context: Two conditional calls about a UHG defamation suit against Dr. Potter: if filed, it would be dismissed as a SLAPP; if it went to trial, UHG would face relentless discovery.
statements.note: Compound conditional; dismissal and discovery predictions.

statements.quote: they would subpoena every record the insurance company ever had about this case, and probably about a bunch of other cases. It will be working to establish the pattern of behavior on the part of UnitedHealth Group in asking for prior authorizations at unreasonable times.
statements.context: Conditional on a trial: the author predicts Dr. Potter's defense would subpoena UHG's records on this and other cases to establish a pattern of unreasonable prior-authorization demands and misleading coverage representations to doctors.
statements.note: Conditional on the case going to trial.

statements.quote: To establish that she's doing this for her own personal gain would also be quite the lift
statements.context: The author assesses UHG's letter claim that Dr. Potter defamed the company for personal gain: proving personal benefit plus knowing, malicious falsehood would be very hard for UHG.
statements.confidence_phrase: would also be quite the lift
statements.note: Borderline: legal-burden analysis with a predictive reading (UHG would fail to prove it).

statements.quote: they're probably stuck with demonstrating actual financial damages specifically related to this doctor statements, which is going to be close to impossible
statements.context: The author argues no per se defamation category applies to UHG, so it would have to prove specific financial damages caused by Dr. Potter's statements, which he predicts is nearly impossible given the company's size and general public opprobrium.
statements.confidence_phrase: probably ... going to be close to impossible
statements.note: Conditional on a suit being filed.

statements.quote: Never will be more emboldened than when United send lawyers after doctor to do reconstructive surgery after breast cancer
statements.context: After screenshots of hateful comments the author received for opposing the murder of UHG's executive, he says the internet's haters will never be more emboldened than by UHG sending lawyers after a breast reconstruction surgeon. Predictive reading: the legal threat will inflame online hostility toward UHG.
statements.note: Garbled sentence; borderline forecast about online reaction.

statements.quote: Yes, the doctor and question is absolutely gonna voluntarily take down her videos, and issue a public apology for ever having falsely claim that UnitedHealth Group called her and asked her to do anything. Oh, wait, that's absolutely not what's gonna happen
statements.context: Closing section. Sarcastic setup followed by the sincere call: Dr. Potter will not take down her videos or issue the public apology that the Clare Locke letter demands.
statements.note: First sentence is sarcasm; the sincere claim is its negation: Potter will not comply with the takedown/apology demand.

statements.quote: UHG gonna hire an expensive law firm—Thomas Clare drafted this letter himself—and the next thing you know, this surgeon will be on stage at the next Super Bowl, bumping hips with Serena Williams, getting down wit Kendrick Lamar, letting the world know that UnitedHealth Group? They not like us.
statements.context: Closing joke: UHG's legal threat will make Dr. Potter famous, ending with her on stage at the next Super Bowl halftime show. The literal claim is a joke; the underlying expectation that the threat backfires (Streisand effect) is logged separately from the opening of the post.
statements.note: Joke/hyperbole; the sincere Streisand-effect expectation is the first statement of this post.

statements.quote: This is the third similarly designed trial. Yes, there will be criticisms
statements.context: Intro to the third randomized trial of accelerated iTBS (SAINT-style) for bipolar depression (Appelbaum et al., UCSD, JAMA Network Open 2025). The author says there will be criticisms, then supplies his own: failed randomization (age and sex imbalance) and an ATHF-based treatment-resistance criterion he calls unserious.
statements.note: Borderline: may refer to the criticisms the author is about to make in this article rather than to external reception of the trial.
